catalog_quote: Stress arguably is not part of Karbi phonology proper, because it never creates a lexical contrast between two morphemes, and a detailed phonetic study of stress is outside the scope of this grammar. ... Grüßner (1978: 23; my translation) remarks that “in syllables with main stress and medium stress, tones are pronounced clearly. In syllables with weak stress, tones become indistinguishable and approximately converge towards Tone 1 [i.e., the low tone].” He continues to link the strength of stress to morpheme type: “the main stress usually resides on the stem syllable, [i.e.] the syllable with the semantically most important function. It [i.e., that syllable] is usually the syllable of a free morpheme. If this [morpheme] is multisyllabic, then the main stress resides on the last syllable.” My own observations match Grüßner’s. There exists an iambic stress pattern in Karbi multisyllabic …

audit.reasoning: The classification (morphological: non-contrastive stress fixed by morpheme class — stem/last syllable of polysyllabic morpheme, prefixes and inflection-like suffixes/enclitics unstressed, in a three-tone language) rests on the dedicated stress section of the standard modern reference grammar (Konnerth 2014, 749 pp), which we hold and in which every quoted sentence was found verbatim at the stated pages (91-93; tone at sec. 3.5, 3.5.8.3 pp. 88-89). Konnerth both translates Gruessner 1978 and confirms the pattern from her own fieldwork, listing the single exception (hala). No instrumental or dedicated stress study of Hills Karbi was found; the one instrumental paper (Konnerth & Teo 2014, downloaded to is on tone and is silent on stress placement while presupposing the same stressed/unstressed distinction. sources.quote: Instrumental study of TONE on monosyllables (2 speakers); no stress-placement rule of its own. Only stress content is a summary of Gruessner (1978: 20-1): the M tone's realization 'depends on other prosodic and morphological factors: a. on a stressed syllable either before a pause (word-finally) ... b. within a word, on a stressed syllable, preceding a L or H tone syllable ...'; and 'the M tone ... is generally sensitive to stress and syllable position, unlike the L and H tones'. Consistent with the stress-tone interaction coded in srule but silent on where stress falls.
